q1.attribution: —Historian's account of mass propaganda in totalitarian states, c. 1920–1945
q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE method of propaganda described in the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the rise of state propaganda in the interwar period.
parts.c: Explain ONE difference between Nazi and Soviet propaganda messages.

sample_answers.a: Both regimes created state monopolies over newspapers, radio, film, and art, using them to manufacture a single approved reality and stage politics as mass spectacle.
sample_answers.b: One cause was new media technology — radio and film could reach entire populations daily for the first time, giving any state that controlled them unprecedented power to shape opinion.
sample_answers.c: Nazi propaganda centered on race — Aryan superiority and Jewish conspiracy — while Soviet propaganda centered on class — the worker's struggle against capitalist exploiters; the enemy was biological in one and economic in the other.

q1.stimulus: Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union were enemies, but they built the same machine: a state monopoly on newspapers, radio, film, and art, all aimed at manufacturing a single reality. Goebbels's ministry and Soviet agitprop both understood that modern media could reach every citizen daily — and both used it to turn politics into spectacle: the Nuremberg rallies, the Stakhanovite campaigns. The content differed — race versus class — but the method, total control of the public image, was identical.

q2.attribution: —Adapted from Joseph Goebbels, Nazi minister of propaganda, speech on propaganda methods, 1934
q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE principle of propaganda Goebbels describes.
parts.b: Explain ONE way the Nazi regime applied such principles after 1933.
parts.c: Explain ONE limitation on the effectiveness of totalitarian propaganda.

sample_answers.a: He describes propaganda as simple, endlessly repeated emotional messaging designed to make people internalize the regime's ideas as their own.
sample_answers.b: The regime applied this through the Reich Chamber of Culture, which controlled all press, radio, film, and art; radios were made cheap and ubiquitous, and rallies and films repeated simple slogans and images.
sample_answers.c: One limitation was lived experience: propaganda claiming prosperity and unity rang hollow against food shortages, bombing raids, and military defeat — and many citizens privately doubted official claims, as diaries and jokes of the period show.

q2.stimulus: [Paraphrase of Goebbels's argument:] Propaganda must be simple, repeated endlessly, and aimed at the emotions rather than the intellect. The essence of propaganda is winning people over to an idea so sincerely that they end by making it their own.

q3.attribution: El Lissitzky, 'Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge,' 1919
q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the poster.
parts.b: Explain ONE way the poster illustrates the methods of revolutionary propaganda.
parts.c: Explain ONE similarity between Soviet posters like this one and Nazi propaganda posters of the 1930s.

sample_answers.a: The poster uses pure abstraction — a sharp red wedge piercing a white circle — with no realistic figures, turning the civil war into a simple geometric struggle of red revolution against white reaction.
sample_answers.b: It shows propaganda reduced to an instantly readable symbol: even illiterate viewers could grasp red-versus-white, demonstrating how the Bolsheviks used avant-garde art to mobilize a largely illiterate population.
sample_answers.c: Both used bold, simple, emotionally charged imagery to divide the world into friend and enemy and to make complex politics instantly legible — abstraction for the Soviets, racial caricature for the Nazis, but the same visual bluntness.

q3.stimulus: El Lissitzky, 'Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge' (1919): a red wedge drives into a white circle — an abstract Bolshevik propaganda poster from the Russian Civil War.
